A new kind of Node library ecosystem

Node.js developers assemble networking, validation, caching, concurrency, observability, and application infrastructure from many packages. Ametherian investigates where consistent contracts and well-defined package boundaries could make that work easier to understand and maintain.
Each package has a clear purpose, documented behavior, explicit limits, and the freedom to be adopted on its own. The ambition is broader than replacing a single HTTP client.
Each family now has preview packages with tests and threat models.
HTTP clients, transports, connection pools, proxies, streaming, retries, deadlines, and cancellation.
Validation, schemas, parsing, serialization, conversion, structured data, and safe handling of untrusted input.
Caching, queues, concurrency, rate limiting, configuration, lifecycle management, and resilience.
Security policy helpers, secure configuration, dependency review, test fixtures, and regression tooling.
Logging, diagnostics, metrics, tracing, typed errors, test utilities, fuzzing helpers, and documentation tooling.

The packages are implemented as previews in this repository, with tests, type declarations and threat models. They are licensed under Apache 2.0, not yet published to npm, and not audited. Anything beyond this needs evidence.

Ametherian builds on the runtime’s established APIs rather than inventing a parallel way to write JavaScript. Compatibility and performance claims will need reproducible evidence before they are published.

The Ametherian project vision: a family of focused JavaScript and TypeScript packages with clear boundaries.
A cohesive ecosystem of focused packages — not one oversized dependency.

Node.js has a mature package ecosystem. It also has recurring friction: overlapping packages, inconsistent contracts, undocumented limits, and security posture that varies by maintainer. Ametherian investigates whether a cohesive family of focused packages can reduce that friction without forcing adoption of one oversized dependency.
The goal is not a single framework. The goal is a set of modules that share conventions, document their behavior, and can be adopted independently.

Ametherian architecture direction: modular packages, shared contracts, explicit Node.js runtime boundaries, and resource safety.
Modular packages, explicit runtime boundaries, shared contracts.
Packages should have one understandable responsibility, declare supported runtime capabilities, and remain useful without unrelated modules.

Shared contracts include typed errors, cancellation, deadlines, resource lifecycle, configuration validation, logging hooks, and documentation of side effects. Shared contracts should reduce fragmentation without circular dependencies or forced dependencies.
Node.js is the initial target. APIs should make runtime assumptions explicit and isolate environment-specific behavior behind adapters where useful. Unsupported capabilities should fail clearly.
Network and stream-oriented packages should define timeouts, maximum sizes, concurrency bounds, backpressure, cancellation, and cleanup. Defaults should be conservative and configurable.

Before stable releases, the project should document supported Node.js versions, module formats, TypeScript support, semantic versioning policy, deprecation windows, and interoperability expectations. Compatibility and performance claims need reproducible tests and benchmark methodology.
The Ametherian security approach: threat modeling, secure engineering practices, vulnerability intelligence, and coordinated disclosure.
Threat models, bounded resources, and evidence-backed claims.
Security is a design and maintenance requirement, not a marketing guarantee. Each package must document trust boundaries, threat model, assumptions, and known limitations.

Threat modeling should consider SSRF, DNS rebinding, redirect policy bypasses, TLS hostname and certificate validation, credential exposure, unsafe parsing, prototype pollution, decompression bombs, unbounded resource use, cache poisoning and isolation, filesystem traversal, concurrency races, and dependency or build-chain compromise.
Reusing mature cryptographic, TLS, compression, and parsing primitives.
Bounding resource use and avoiding secret logging.
Tracking dependency provenance and adding regression tests for confirmed vulnerabilities.
Requiring human review for security-sensitive fixes.

Vulnerability intelligence may draw on OSV, GitHub Security Advisories, NVD, CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, Node.js security advisories, and upstream advisories. Any ingestion must preserve source attribution, timestamps, affected-version ranges, confidence, and freshness. Intelligence informs review and testing; it must not trigger unreviewed production changes.

Ametherian security policy: reporting vulnerabilities, and the intended security process for future packages.
Reporting status and the intended security process.
This policy applies to this repository, including its preview packages, and to future release repositories.
Do not open a public issue for a security vulnerability. Report it privately to the maintainers. Security-sensitive details must not be posted publicly before coordinated disclosure.

There are currently no released packages and no security-audited guarantees. If a vulnerability is found in the site infrastructure or repository configuration, it should be reported following this policy.
